<meta>continues from previous page: ...The creator Mind, indeed, together with</meta> the Word, containing the circles, and turning its own machine with rapid speed, bent it and commanded it to revolve from a beginning without beginning to an end without end. For it always begins there where it leaves off. The circulation of all these things, just as the Mind itself willed, formed from the lower elements animals lacking reason; for it did not provide them with reason. The air brought forth flying things, and the water brought forth swimming things. The water and the earth were also separated from one another in the manner that had pleased the Mind. The earth subsequently brought forth the living beings it had contained within: namely, quadrupeds, creeping things, wild beasts, both of the field and domestic. 

But the Father of all, existing as intellect, life, and radiance, procreated man similar to himself, and he congratulated him as if he were his own son. For he was beautiful and bore the image of his Father. For God, delighted by his own true form, granted all his works for human use. Man, however, <margin>Note the sin of the philosophers <unclear>what it may be</unclear></margin> when he had considered the procreation of all things in his Father, he also wanted to fashion things. Whence he fell down from the contemplation of the Father to the sphere of generation. And although he had the power of all things within himself, he observed the handiwork of the seven governors. These, rejoicing in the meditation of the human mind, each shared their own order

<summary>This passage describes the creation of the animal kingdom from the lower elements and the unique birth of man, created by the Father as a reflection of His own image. It further explores man's desire to act as a creator, leading to his descent from divine contemplation into the sphere of physical generation.</summary>
<keywords>Hermes Trismegistus, creation, intellect, sphere of generation, seven governors, human image</keywords>
